 Congress slow to change on daylight-saving time – and that's a good thing 
 The Journal Gazette Editorial Board

 The 119th Congress has developed a well-earned reputation for accomplishing very little. But its apparent refusal to make daylight-saving time permanent may be one of its more sensible decisions.
 It’s not hyperbole to say most Americans are sick of losing an hour or gaining an hour in spring and fall. But there’s a difference between inconvenience and hastening a solution that could make matters worse.
 The House has passed legislation making daylight-saving time permanent, and President Donald Trump wants the Senate to follow suit. But several Republican senators have resisted. Indiana Sen. Todd Young says the legislation appears to be a nonstarter.
 The problem isn’t the desire to stop changing clocks. It’s the assumption that permanent daylight-saving time is the best alternative.
 The American Academy of Sleep Medicine favors permanent standard time, arguing that it better aligns our daily schedules with the body’s natural circadian rhythms. Morning sunlight helps regulate sleep and wakefulness. Moving an hour of daylight into the evening comes at the expense of that morning light.
 Consider what permanent daylight- saving time would mean in Fort Wayne. Around the winter solstice, sunrise would come shortly after 9 a.m. Children would be traveling to school in darkness, while many workers would begin their days before sunrise.
 And we’ve tried this before, with less than enthusiastic results.
 Congress adopted permanent daylight-saving time in January 1974 during the national energy crisis. The experiment quickly lost public support, in part because parents worried about children going to school in the dark. Congress reversed course that October.
 Indiana has its own peculiar history with the clock.
 Until 2006, most of the state, including Allen County, observed Eastern Standard Time year-round. That changed after a contentious 2005 legislative battle, when Gov. Mitch Daniels argued that Indiana’s unusual arrangement created confusion for businesses operating across state lines. The legislation passed the Indiana House by a single vote.
 Daniels’ argument was primarily about economic coordination, not the supposed benefits of additional evening sunlight. And the state’s decision reflected a legitimate desire to make doing business with the rest of the country easier.
 But two decades later, the discussion should also account for what researchers have learned about the relationship between daylight, sleep and health.
 None of this means the current system is ideal. But finding a better solution deserves careful consideration, not a rush to enact whichever proposal sounds most appealing on the surface.
 The Senate should examine that alternative rather than simply rubber- stamp the House bill. Sometimes elected officials have an obligation to resist a popular demand when evidence and experience counsel otherwise. Indiana could even choose permanent standard time under existing law, ending twice-yearly clock changes.
 Congress cannot change the Earth’s rotation or the seasons. But it should avoid putting daylight in the wrong place.
